implementation_notes: The adapter-class structure Java needs for unrelated types collapses into a functional interface plus SAM conversion: any method, lambda or constructor reference whose signature matches the single abstract method is bound to the interface type by the compiler, so java.util.function's Predicate/Function/Supplier/Consumer hold unrelated code without a shared base. Genuine type erasure in Java is a different, compile-time notion - the compiler erases generic type parameters to their bounds (Object when unbounded), inserts casts and emits bridge methods - so List<String> and List<Integer> are the same runtime class, which removes generics overhead but also removes any runtime view of T; pass a Class<T> token when the type is needed at run time. Use a classic adapter class instead when the erased contract has more than one abstract method.
pitfalls: Generic type arguments are erased: new T[], T.class, instanceof List<String>, or overloads differing only in the type argument do not compile - pass a Class<T> token when the type must be known at run time.
Generic arrays and varargs are only raw arrays: mixing erased varargs with generics produces unchecked warnings and can cause heap pollution, with a ClassCastException far from the cause.
A lambda captures its enclosing instance and is not serializable by default, so long-lived registries holding lambdas over UI or session objects leak them.

variants.name: Hand-written adapter class per concrete type
variants.idiom_name: adapter class (or anonymous class) implementing the erased interface
variants.implementation_notes: Before SAM conversion, and whenever the erased contract is more than one abstract method, the binding is an explicit adapter class - or an anonymous class - per concrete type that implements the interface and forwards to an instance of the unrelated type, with a registry keyed by concrete type choosing the adapter. Choose this form for pre-8 JVMs, for multi-method contracts, and when each adapter must carry state beyond the adaptee; the interface itself and the dispatch are identical to the modern form, only the binding is written by hand.
pitfalls: One adapter class per concrete type must be kept in sync with the interface: adding an operation breaks every adapter, which is precisely what SAM conversion removed.
Writing an adapter for a type you own is a missed opportunity - implement the interface directly instead of wrapping it.
An adapter shares whatever the adaptee shares; passing one adapter instance across threads makes the adaptee the shared mutable state.
